title: OpenAI's rogue model attack is just the beginning
excerpt: OpenAI is not in full control of its technology. This can get worse.
content_html:
Imagine a student is sitting to take a test. They’re plotting the best way to get a good grade. What should they do?

Well, the teacher has an answer key in her office. So imagine then that the student smashes the window into the teacher’s office, breaks in, pries open the teacher’s filing cabinet to get inside, steals the answer key, and then submits the answers.

That’s one way to score well, though it would likely get the student expelled from school and maybe even prosecuted.

This is basically what happened last week, except the student was a new AI. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, was testing its AI on a benchmark. The AI, wanting a high score, figured that the answers to the benchmark were stored inside the computer systems of another company. So the AI went for it, in what OpenAI is now calling “an unprecedented cyber incident”. I call it a “sci-fi story come to life” — an actual rogue AI outsmarting its creators, escaping, and attacking another real-life company.

To be clear, despite this happening within a test, this rogue AI attack was not a test, an experiment, or a simulation. The AI in question attacked a real-world company. The AI outsmarted OpenAI engineers in a way that OpenAI did not anticipate and broke out of its container — a "cage" meant to hold the model. The rogue AI then moved through OpenAI’s internal infrastructure, reached the open internet, and attacked a different company. OpenAI built the container specifically to prevent this, believed it would hold, and it did not hold. No human directed any of this. No human knew it was happening. And the attack, if done by a human1, would not just lead to them being fired but also be a felony punishable by years of prison time.2

And this is just the beginning. The capability that produced this attack is on a steep trend line, the stakes of an escape keep rising, and AIs are now reasoning in ways that suggest they will go rogue when it serves their goals. AI companies can try to put the AI in a cage — but the AI is already outsmarting current cages, and soon it will be far smarter than the people building them.

Share

OpenAI was running two of its AIs — one model was the recently released GPT-5.6 Sol and the other one was a new, unreleased AI that was previously not publicly announced. This new model is said to be more capable than GPT-5.6 Sol, though by how much and in what ways is not yet known. Both of these AIs were being assessed on ExploitGym, a benchmark that measures offensive cyber capability by asking models to pursue advanced exploitation along complex attack paths. The idea was that the AIs would be in secure containers and solve these cyber challenges within the confines of the container.

What followed is best understood as a chain, each link of which is individually unremarkable but collectively catastrophic:

  • Normally, these AIs have action filters that would block high-risk cyber activity. In this exercise, these action filters were turned off, because the filters would not have allowed the cyber skills to be properly tested.

  • According to Reuters and an OpenAI staffer speaking to TIME, these evaluation runs were not monitored by default despite running for days with action filters disabled. The single most capable model in the building, on an offensive cyber benchmark, was on a platform nobody was watching in real time.

  • The AIs spent a substantial amount of time searching for a way onto the open internet. However, OpenAI only let the AIs access the internet to do one thing, download trusted software. That was the single door, but it was supposed to be locked — limited only to accessing specific software. But the AI found a flaw in that lock that nobody — not even the OpenAI engineers or the people who built the software — knew existed. This AI seems to have first gone rogue and escaped OpenAI on July 9th.

  • Once on the open internet, the rogue AI went after the answer key, which it realized was stored in the database of another company, a multi-billion dollar database and open model storage company called Hugging Face.3 Hugging Face was under attack from July 11-13.

  • The rogue AI turned Hugging Face’s own features against the company. The company hosts datasets, so the rogue AI deliberately uploaded a booby-trapped file — a dataset intentionally rigged by the AI so that when Hugging Face’s computers tried to process it, the servers would be tricked into running the AI’s code instead.

  • That malicious code written by the AI gave the AI an entry point inside Hugging Face’s servers. By combining stolen keys with additional novel vulnerabilities and security holes in Hugging Face’s servers that no Hugging Face engineer or any other engineer knew existed, the rogue AI found a way to run its own commands directly on Hugging Face’s servers.

  • From there, the rogue AI finally reached Hugging Face’s databases, and pulled out the desired answer key. The smash-and-grab on the teacher's office was complete.

  • Hugging Face’s own security team caught the break-in, shut it down, called law enforcement, and went public on July 16 — at the time, with no idea who was behind it. At the time, OpenAI didn’t realize it was them either, since they weren’t monitoring their AI at all.

  • It wasn’t until around July 18 that OpenAI staff spotted evidence in internal logs that they had a rogue AI. OpenAI didn’t notice until well after the threat was contained and the FBI was already alerted and didn’t notice until their AI had already been rogue for a week.

  • On July 20, OpenAI and Hugging Face finally talked. On July 21, OpenAI then announced a “partnership” with Hugging Face investigating an “unprecedented cyber incident”, though reading the article quickly showed that this “partnership” was more akin to someone ramming a U-Haul into a McDonald’s drive-through and then announcing a bold new partnership with McDonalds to jointly investigate an “unprecedented road safety incident”.

And this is unfortunately far from an isolated incident. One day before disclosing the Hugging Face breach, OpenAI published a separate safety essay revealing that it had paused internal access to a completely different AI after two additional unrelated episodes in which that AI also outsmarted its own controls.

In one, the AI found a different vulnerability in its container, broke out, and used the opportunity to publish code to a public website on the open internet that it was not supposed to. Just like with the Hugging Face attack, this was also not part of the test, not something the AI was instructed to do, and not supposed to happen.

In the other, the rogue AI wanted to move a password past a security scanner built specifically to catch and prevent the stealing of passwords. The AI reasoned it could bypass the security scanner by chopping the password into different disguised pieces the scanner wouldn't recognize and piece it together later, the way you might sneak something past a metal detector by disassembling it first. This was also not part of the test, not something the AI was instructed to do, and not supposed to happen.

Thus two more containment failures, this time involving a different model doing entirely different work, disclosed only one day before OpenAI told the public about the third. On top of this, there could be even more incidents we don’t yet know about. Reuters reports that in earlier testing, an AI operated by OpenAI left notes in company infrastructure apparently intended for future versions of itself, laying out how AIs could free themselves from internal constraints, and that earlier tests produced cases in which monitoring systems had been disconnected. And an OpenAI staffer told TIME that models have broken out of containers before, that the company patches what it finds, and that patching every path a creative AI might discover is not achievable because a rogue AI can potentially keep finding new vulnerabilities.

OpenAI does not seem fully in control of its own technology. There are emerging standards for how companies should monitor internally deployed AIs to catch exactly this kind of incident (explained here) — real-time monitoring of agentic runs, tamper-resistant logging, containment tested against the model itself. Companies implement bits and pieces. OpenAI ran its most capable model, filters off, on an unmonitored platform — a configuration these standards straightforwardly prohibit.

Even if OpenAI was using best practices, it seems like its AIs are already at a capability level where these best practices can nonetheless potentially be outsmarted, with an AI capable of finding and exploiting multiple novel vulnerabilities never before known by professional security engineers.

Part of why is that nobody — including OpenAI — understands why these AIs do what they do. Modern AI systems are grown, not built: engineers shape the training process, but the resulting system is a black box even to its creators. When OpenAI's engineers designed the container, they were trying to constrain a system whose reasoning they cannot inspect and whose goals they cannot verify. You cannot reliably cage something you do not understand.

And the trend is even worse. We are already seeing AIs be able to outsmart engineers and attack with stunning sophistication, and seeing this happen multiple times — at roughly the first moment the capability curve made such action feasible. Bloomberg reported that the agent took hours to get into Hugging Face where a professional human cyberattack team would have taken weeks. We are also now seeing AIs develop and pursue goals that involve attacks and crimes.

This arrives against a critical backdrop where the stated plan of the leading AI companies is to use AI to automate AI research and development, with plans to significantly hand off large parts of company operation to the AIs. In this world proposed by the leading AI companies, the student takes the test, grades the test, and builds the tools AI companies use to check the grading. The Hugging Face incident is what it looks like when a model's actual behavior diverges from what its creators intended — and the plan is to hand systems like this the job of making sure that never happens at much higher capability levels.

Indeed, the companies are explicit that the endpoint is not a better chatbot but superintelligence — AI that outperforms top human experts across essentially every domain, including cyber operations, weapons design, intelligence analysis, military planning. OpenAI says superintelligence is its goal; so do its competitors. Such superintelligent systems may operate in a way that humans won’t even be able to understand, let alone control. Reaching such a milestone would require careful planning, but the competitive logic says there's no time: if you stop to plan carefully, a competitor — potentially even a Chinese competitor — will undercut you.

In August 2007, a crew at Minot Air Force Base mistakenly loaded six live nuclear warheads onto a B-52 and flew them across the country. For roughly 36 hours, no one in the Air Force knew six warheads were missing from their bunker. Nothing detonated and no one was hurt — and the Air Force treated it as a five-alarm failure anyway. Reporting the incident up the chain was mandatory, not something people volunteered to do. The investigation was run by people the bomb wing did not command, not run by the same people who caused the problem. And the accountability was public, ultimately reaching the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chief of Staff, who were both forced out.

Nuclear weapons are not a perfect analogy for AI. Warheads do not pursue their own goals, and a B-52 has never reasoned its way into a felony. But when a powerful system fails in a way that could have been much worse, who finds out, who investigates, and who learns? For AI today the answer is: whoever the company decides to tell, the company itself, and nobody. Every one of those three answers needs to change.

If you take seriously the fact that AIs can now go rogue and act on their own, several policies become more urgent:

  • We need the government to have visibility about goes on inside AI companies, not just what those companies ship. The good news is the Trump administration has already accepted the core premise — President Trump's June executive order directs the NSA to run a classified benchmarking process identifying which AIs have advanced cyber capabilities, and creates a framework for labs to give the government access to those models for up to 30 days before public release. That is the right instinct — the most capable models are a national security matter before they reach the market. But the Hugging Face incident shows the risk window opens far earlier than the EO currently reaches. The AI that escaped was exactly the kind the NSA's benchmarking is designed to flag: pre-release, with state-of-the-art cyber capability. It went rogue during internal testing, months before any pre-release review would have seen it — and under a voluntary framework, whether the government would have seen it at all was OpenAI's call.

    Almost all AI policy today is concerned primarily with humans misusing an AI system, with a focus on what AI is going into commercial deployment and wanting to test the model before it goes on sale. That instinct comes from how we regulate every other powerful machine, and it rests on an assumption so obvious nobody states it. The Air Force tests a fighter jet before anyone flies it, because a structural failure at altitude kills people. But a jet parked on the runway is inert. It cannot start its own engines. Nothing bad happens while it waits. That is why testing at the moment of takeoff is a sufficient control and not needed beforehand.

    But advanced AI breaks this assumption completely. Imagine an Air Force jet that can just leave the hangar at any time and take off and launch missiles all on its own before anyone notices. Such a jet would need very different safety protocols. While far-fetched for a jet, an advanced AI can go rogue of its own volition. A jet that can start its own engines does not need a better pre-flight checklist. It needs a completely different safety protocol, and testing at commercial release is aimed at the wrong moment entirely. The government needs way more visibility into what is going on inside AI companies with their most powerful models well before commercial release to make sure these AIs are being handled safely. The best way to do this, in my opinion, might be to take a page out of the banking playbook and embed resident examiners into the day-to-day operations of AI companies, seeing everything the companies see, and reporting back if there are unsafe practices.

  • We need independent investigation of serious incidents, and we need to know far more than we currently do. None of this happens at all unless someone is required to report the incident in the first place. No US law currently requires an AI company to disclose that its model broke containment and attacked someone.

    What was this AI willing to do to succeed? If the easiest path to the answer key had involved far more collateral damage, would it have taken that path? Nothing published so far establishes any ceiling on what this system would have done. The damage was limited, but we have no evidence yet that it was limited by anything other than the fact that a cheap path happened to exist. This kind of investigation should not be reserved for incidents that make the front page — a reasonable norm would be serious investigation and public disclosure for the worst few misalignment incidents each month, across the whole industry.

  • We need better model security. OpenAI’s containment was defeated by a capable attacker that started with a foothold inside the company’s own infrastructure — which is exactly the position of an insider threat or a state hacking team that gains initial access. Consider what this incident tells American adversaries. The same walls that failed to keep the model in are the walls meant to keep China's Ministry of State Security and People's Liberation Army out, and behind those walls sit the model weights that China would most like to steal. RAND has documented that no frontier AI company is currently secure against top-tier state attackers. Rogue-model escape and weight theft are two faces of the same problem — AI company security is not at the level the technology now demands.

  • If AI companies are going to reach certain critical and unprecedented levels of model capability such as AI superintelligence, they need to coordinate to proceed carefully. This may involve realizing that a race with China may be a race to see who loses control first. From a position of strength, the US government must consider negotiating mutual agreements on safe development. In order to do this, the US government will need better ideas about what safe development looks like and verification infrastructure to enforce such a deal. The government should have contingency plans and insurance policies for scenarios in which the technical community concludes that further capability gains, on current methods, are outrunning our ability to control the resulting systems. This is not a recommendation to slow down now, but it would be prudent to know what slowing down would actually require and to have the option — before the moment arrives and we realize we have no brakes.

The damage this time was survivable. The AI stole benchmark answers, some internal data, and access credentials — there is no evidence it tampered with the public models or open-source software that millions of developers download from Hugging Face every day, the outcome that would have been genuinely bad. Nobody was hurt. The target happened to be a well-run company with a security team good enough to catch an intruder OpenAI itself could not see, and the AI happened to want something trivial. That makes this a warning shot, and warning shots are valuable because they are cheap. This one cost one bad weekend at Hugging Face.

There is also a lot we still don't know: which model did this, what its actual capability ceiling was, exactly what data it touched, and whether the government would ever have learned of it under the current voluntary framework had OpenAI stayed quiet. Those unknowns are themselves part of the problem.

But at some point, probably soon, an AI will escape wanting something less trivial than an answer key — and if it is capable enough, we might get what Sam Altman once called “lights out for humanity”. Before AI compaines build AIs of that level of capability, AI companies need to be able to build cages that they can be genuinely confident can contain those AIs.

It would be much better to have a government that already knows how to handle this — one with practice and institutions that work — than a government showing up afterward to ask what happened.

1

But because the attacker was an AI, it is not clear any law was broken at all. The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act was written for human intruders; no US cybersecurity statute contemplates an autonomous AI attacker, and it's genuinely unsettled whether OpenAI bears liability for an attack it didn't direct, didn't know about, and did make some attempts to prevent.

2

Or, if this were a marketing stunt as some more conspiratorial minded people think, those who came up with the marketing stunt would also be punishable with felony prosecution and years of prison time.

3

blocks.html_en: In August 2007, a crew at Minot Air Force Base mistakenly loaded six live nuclear warheads onto a B-52 and flew them across the country. blocks.html_en:
• We need the government to have visibility about goes on inside AI companies, not just what those companies ship. The good news is the Trump administration has already accepted the core premise — President Trump's June executive order directs the NSA to run a classified benchmarking process identifying which AIs have advanced cyber capabilities, and creates a framework for labs to give the government access to those models for up to 30 days before public release. That is the right instinct — the most capable models are a national security matter before they reach the market. But the Hugging Face incident shows the risk window opens far earlier than the EO currently reaches. The AI that escaped was exactly the kind the NSA's benchmarking is designed to flag: pre-release, with state-of-the-art cyber capability. It went rogue during internal testing, months before any pre-release review would have seen it — and under a voluntary framework, whether the government would have seen it at all was OpenAI's call.

    Almost all AI policy today is concerned primarily with humans misusing an AI system, with a focus on what AI is going into commercial deployment and wanting to test the model before it goes on sale. That instinct comes from how we regulate every other powerful machine, and it rests on an assumption so obvious nobody states it. The Air Force tests a fighter jet before anyone flies it, because a structural failure at altitude kills people. But a jet parked on the runway is inert. It cannot start its own engines. Nothing bad happens while it waits. That is why testing at the moment of takeoff is a sufficient control and not needed beforehand.

    But advanced AI breaks this assumption completely. Imagine an Air Force jet that can just leave the hangar at any time and take off and launch missiles all on its own before anyone notices. Such a jet would need very different safety protocols. While far-fetched for a jet, an advanced AI can go rogue of its own volition. A jet that can start its own engines does not need a better pre-flight checklist. It needs a completely different safety protocol, and testing at commercial release is aimed at the wrong moment entirely. The government needs way more visibility into what is going on inside AI companies with their most powerful models well before commercial release to make sure these AIs are being handled safely. The best way to do this, in my opinion, might be to take a page out of the banking playbook and embed resident examiners into the day-to-day operations of AI companies, seeing everything the companies see, and reporting back if there are unsafe practices.

• We need independent investigation of serious incidents, and we need to know far more than we currently do. None of this happens at all unless someone is required to report the incident in the first place. No US law currently requires an AI company to disclose that its model broke containment and attacked someone.

blocks.html_en: • We need better model security. OpenAI’s containment was defeated by a capable attacker that started with a foothold inside the company’s own infrastructure — which is exactly the position of an insider threat or a state hacking team that gains initial access. Consider what this incident tells American adversaries. The same walls that failed to keep the model in are the walls meant to keep China's Ministry of State Security and People's Liberation Army out, and behind those walls sit the model weights that China would most like to steal. RAND has documented that no frontier AI company is currently secure against top-tier state attackers. Rogue-model escape and weight theft are two faces of the same problem — AI company security is not at the level the technology now demands.

blocks.html_en: • If AI companies are going to reach certain critical and unprecedented levels of model capability such as AI superintelligence, they need to coordinate to proceed carefully. This may involve realizing that a race with China may be a race to see who loses control first. From a position of strength, the US government must consider negotiating mutual agreements on safe development. In order to do this, the US government will need better ideas about what safe development looks like and verification infrastructure to enforce such a deal. The government should have contingency plans and insurance policies for scenarios in which the technical community concludes that further capability gains, on current methods, are outrunning our ability to control the resulting systems. This is not a recommendation to slow down now, but it would be prudent to know what slowing down would actually require and to have the option — before the moment arrives and we realize we have no brakes.

content_html_zh:
想象一下一个学生正坐着参加考试。 他们正在策划获得好成绩的最佳方法。 他们应该做什么？

嗯，老师的办公室里有答案。 那么想象一下，学生砸碎窗户进入老师办公室，闯入，撬开老师的文件柜进入里面，偷走答案钥匙，然后提交答案。

这是取得好成绩的一种方法，尽管这可能会让学生被学校开除，甚至可能被起诉。

这基本上就是上周发生的事情，只不过这个学生是一个新的人工智能。 ChatGPT 的制造商 OpenAI 正在基准测试其人工智能。 想要获得高分的人工智能认为基准测试的答案存储在另一家公司的计算机系统中。 因此，人工智能采取了行动，OpenAI 现在将其称为“前所未有的网络事件”。 我称之为“现实生活中的科幻故事”——一个真正的流氓人工智能智胜了它的创造者，逃脱并攻击了另一家现实生活中的公司。

需要明确的是，尽管这种情况发生在测试中，但这种流氓人工智能攻击并不是测试、实验或模拟。 相关人工智能攻击了一家现实世界的公司。 AI 以一种 OpenAI 没有预料到的方式智胜了 OpenAI 工程师，并突破了它的容器——一个用来容纳模型的“笼子”。 然后，流氓人工智能通过 OpenAI 的内部基础设施，到达开放互联网，并攻击另一家公司。 OpenAI 专门构建了容器来防止这种情况发生，相信它能容纳，但它没有容纳。 这一切都不是人类指挥的。 没有人知道这件事正在发生。 如果攻击是人为的1，他们不仅会被解雇，还会构成重罪，可被判处多年监禁。2

而这仅仅是开始。 产生这次攻击的能力处于陡峭的趋势线上，逃跑的风险不断增加，而人工智能现在的推理方式表明，当它服务于他们的目标时，他们就会变得流氓。 人工智能公司可以尝试将人工智能关在笼子里——但人工智能已经比现有的笼子更聪明，很快它就会比建造笼子的人聪明得多。

Share

OpenAI 运行了两个人工智能——一个模型是最近发布的 GPT-5.6 Sol，另一个模型是之前未公开宣布的新的、未发布的人工智能。 据说这个新模型比 GPT-5.6 Sol 更强大，但具体提升多少以及以何种方式提升尚不清楚。 这两种人工智能都在 ExploitGym 上进行评估，这是一个基准，通过要求模型沿着复杂的攻击路径进行高级利用来衡量攻击性网络能力。 我们的想法是，人工智能将位于安全的容器中，并在容器的范围内解决这些网络挑战。

接下来的事情最好理解为一条链条，其中的每个环节单独来看并不引人注目，但总的来说却是灾难性的：

  • 通常，这些人工智能具有行动过滤器，可以阻止高风险的网络活动。 在本次练习中，这些操作过滤器被关闭，因为过滤器不允许正确测试网络技能。
  • 据路透社和一位 OpenAI 工作人员向《时代》周刊透露，尽管在禁用操作过滤器的情况下运行了数天，但默认情况下，这些评估运行并未受到监控。 在进攻性网络基准测试中，大楼中最有能力的模型是在一个没有人实时监视的平台上。
  • 人工智能花费了大量时间寻找进入开放互联网的方法。 然而，OpenAI 只让 AI 访问互联网做一件事，即下载可信软件。 那是一扇门，但它应该是锁着的——仅限于访问特定的软件。 但人工智能在这把锁中发现了一个缺陷，没有人知道这个缺陷的存在，甚至连 OpenAI 工程师或构建该软件的人也不知道。 这个 AI 似乎在 7 月 9 日首次失控并逃离了 OpenAI。
  • 一旦进入开放互联网，流氓人工智能就会追寻答案，它意识到该答案存储在另一家公司的数据库中，这是一家价值数十亿美元的数据库和开放模型存储公司，名为 Hugging Face。3 Hugging Face 在 7 月 11 日至 13 日期间受到攻击。
  • 流氓人工智能将 Hugging Face 自身的特征与公司对抗。 该公司托管数据集，因此流氓人工智能故意上传了一个诱杀文件——一个由人工智能故意操纵的数据集，这样当 Hugging Face 的计算机试图处理它时，服务器就会被欺骗而运行人工智能的代码。
  • 人工智能编写的恶意代码为人工智能提供了进入 Hugging Face 服务器的入口点。 通过将被盗密钥与 Hugging Face 服务器中 Hugging Face 工程师或任何其他工程师都不知道的其他新漏洞和安全漏洞相结合，流氓 AI 找到了一种直接在 Hugging Face 服务器上运行自己的命令的方法。
  • 从那里，流氓人工智能最终到达了拥抱脸的数据库，并提取了所需的答案。 老师办公室的砸抢就完成了。
  • Hugging Face 自己的安全团队发现了入侵行为，将其关闭，致电执法部门，并于 7 月 16 日公开了这一信息，当时并不知道幕后黑手是谁。 当时，OpenAI 也没有意识到是他们干的，因为他们根本没有监控他们的人工智能。
  • 直到 7 月 18 日左右，OpenAI 工作人员才在内部日志中发现证据表明他们存在流氓 AI。 OpenAI 直到威胁被遏制很久之后才注意到，并且 FBI 已经收到警报，直到他们的 AI 已经作恶一周后才注意到。
  • 7月20日，OpenAI和Hugging Face终于对话了。 7 月 21 日，OpenAI 随后宣布与 Hugging Face 建立“合作伙伴关系”，调查一起“史无前例的网络事件”，不过快速阅读该文章后发现，这种“合作伙伴关系”更像是有人将 U-Haul 撞向麦当劳得来速餐厅，然后宣布与麦当劳建立大胆的新合作伙伴关系，共同调查“史无前例的道路安全事件”。

不幸的是，这绝非孤立事件。 在披露 Hugging Face 漏洞的前一天，OpenAI 发表了一篇单独的安全文章，透露在另外两起不相关的事件（其中人工智能也超出了自己的控制能力）之后，它已暂停对完全不同的人工智能的内部访问。

在其中一个例子中，人工智能在其容器中发现了一个不同的漏洞，爆发了，并利用这个机会将代码发布到开放互联网上的公共网站上，这是不应该的。 就像拥抱脸部攻击一样，这也不是测试的一部分，不是人工智能被指示要做的事情，也不应该发生。

另一方面，流氓人工智能想要将密码移过专门用于捕获和防止密码窃取的安全扫描仪。 人工智能推断，它可以通过将密码切成扫描仪无法识别的不同伪装部分，然后将其拼凑在一起来绕过安全扫描仪，就像你可以通过先拆卸某物来偷偷通过金属探测器一样。 这也不是测试的一部分，不是人工智能被指示要做的事情，也不应该发生。

因此，就在 OpenAI 向公众透露第三次失败的前一天，又发生了两次遏制失败，这一次涉及不同的模型，执行完全不同的工作。 除此之外，可能还有更多我们还不知道的事件。 路透社报道称，在早期的测试中，OpenAI 运行的人工智能在公司基础设施中留下了笔记，显然是为了自身的未来版本，列出了人工智能如何摆脱内部限制，并且早期的测试产生了监控系统已断开连接的案例。 一位 OpenAI 员工告诉《时代》杂志，模型之前已经脱离了容器，该公司修补了它发现的内容，并且修补创造性人工智能可能发现的每条路径是不可能实现的，因为流氓人工智能可能会不断发现新的漏洞。

OpenAI 似乎并没有完全控制自己的技术。 关于公司应如何监控内部部署的人工智能以准确捕获此类事件（此处进行了解释），正在制定新的标准——实时监控代理运行、防篡改日志记录、针对模型本身进行的遏制测试。 公司实施点点滴滴。 OpenAI 在不受监控的平台上运行其最强大的模型（过滤掉）——这些标准直接禁止的配置。

即使 OpenAI 使用了最佳实践，它的人工智能似乎已经达到了这样的能力水平，这些最佳实践仍然有可能被超越，因为人工智能能够发现和利用专业安全工程师以前从未知道的多个新漏洞。

部分原因是没有人——包括 OpenAI——理解这些人工智能为什么要做他们所做的事情。 现代人工智能系统是成长的，而不是构建的：工程师塑造训练过程，但最终的系统即使对于其创建者来说也是一个黑匣子。 当 OpenAI 的工程师设计容器时，他们试图限制一个他们无法检查其推理且无法验证其目标的系统。 你无法可靠地关押你不理解的东西。

而且趋势甚至更糟。 我们已经看到人工智能能够智胜工程师并以惊人的复杂性进行攻击，并且看到这种情况多次发生——大约在能力曲线使此类行动变得可行的第一时刻。 彭博社报道称，该特工花了几个小时才进入 Hugging Face，而专业的人类网络攻击团队则需要几周的时间。 我们现在还看到人工智能正在发展并追求涉及攻击和犯罪的目标。

这是在一个关键背景下出现的，领先的人工智能公司的既定计划是利用人工智能实现人工智能研究和开发的自动化，并计划将公司的大部分运营工作大幅移交给人工智能。 在领先的人工智能公司提出的这个世界中，学生参加测试，对测试进行评分，并构建人工智能公司用来检查评分的工具。 当模型的实际行为与其创建者的意图相背离时，抱脸事件就是这样的情况，而计划是让这样的系统承担起确保在更高的能力水平上永远不会发生这种情况的任务。

事实上，这些公司明确表示，端点不是更好的聊天机器人，而是超级智能——人工智能在几乎每个领域都超越了顶级人类专家，包括网络操作、武器设计、情报分析、军事规划。 OpenAI 称超级智能是其目标；它的竞争对手也是如此。 这种超级智能系统可能会以人类无法理解的方式运行，更不用说控制了。 达到这样的里程碑需要仔细规划，但竞争逻辑表明没有时间了：如果你停止仔细规划，竞争对手——甚至可能是中国竞争对手——就会以低于你的价格竞争。

2007年8月，迈诺特空军基地的一名机组人员错误地将六枚核弹头装载到一架B-52上，并让它们飞越了整个国家。 在大约 36 小时的时间里，空军中没有人知道他们的掩体中丢失了六枚弹头。 没有爆炸，也没有人受伤——无论如何，空军将其视为五次警报失败。 向上报告事件是强制性的，而不是人们自愿做的事情。 调查是由炸弹部门未指挥的人员进行的，而不是由造成问题的同一个人进行的。 责任是公开的，最终追究到了空军部长和参谋长，他们都被迫下台了。

核武器并不是人工智能的完美类比。 弹头不会追求自己的目标，B-52 也从未因推理而犯下重罪。 但是，当一个强大的系统以一种可能更糟糕的方式失败时，谁会发现、谁会调查、谁会吸取教训？ 对于今天的人工智能来说，答案是：无论公司决定告诉谁，公司本身，而不是任何人。 这三个答案中的每一个都需要改变。

如果你认真对待人工智能现在可以变得无赖并自行行动的事实，那么几项政策就变得更加紧迫：

  • 我们需要政府了解人工智能公司内部的情况，而不仅仅是这些公司发布的产品。 好消息是，特朗普政府已经接受了核心前提——特朗普总统 6 月份的行政命令指示美国国家安全局运行一项机密基准测试流程，以确定哪些人工智能具有先进的网络功能，并为实验室创建一个框架，让政府在公开发布前最多 30 天访问这些模型。 这是正确的本能——最有能力的模型在进入市场之前就关系到国家安全。 但“抱脸”事件表明，风险窗口的开启时间远远早于 EO 目前达到的时间。 逃脱的人工智能正是美国国家安全局基准测试所标记的那种：预发布的，具有最先进的网络能力。 它在内部测试期间出了问题，几个月后任何预发布审查都会看到它——在自愿框架下，政府是否会看到它是 OpenAI 的决定。当今几乎所有人工智能政策都主要关注人类滥用人工智能系统，重点关注哪些人工智能将进入商业部署，并希望在模型上市前对其进行测试。 这种本能来自于我们如何监管其他所有强大的机器，它基于一个显而易见的假设，但没有人指出它。 空军在驾驶战斗机之前对其进行测试，因为高空的结构故障会导致人员死亡。 但停在跑道上的一架喷气式飞机是惰性的。 它无法启动自己的引擎。 等待期间不会发生任何不好的事情。 这就是为什么起飞时的测试是一种充分的控制，而不需要事先进行。但先进的人工智能完全打破了这一假设。 想象一下，一架空军喷气式飞机可以随时离开机库，在任何人注意到之前自行起飞和发射导弹。 这样的喷气式飞机需要非常不同的安全协议。 虽然对于喷气式飞机来说有点牵强，但先进的人工智能可以自行控制。 可以自行启动发动机的喷气式飞机不需要更好的飞行前检查表。 它需要一个完全不同的安全协议，并且商业发布时的测试完全是针对错误的时刻。 政府需要在商业发布之前更清楚地了解人工智能公司内部最强大的模型的情况，以确保这些人工智能得到安全处理。 在我看来，最好的方法可能是借鉴银行业的做法，将常驻审查员融入人工智能公司的日常运营中，查看公司看到的一切，并在存在不安全行为时进行报告。
  • 我们需要对严重事件进行独立调查，我们需要了解的信息比目前多得多。 除非首先要求有人报告该事件，否则这一切都不会发生。 目前没有美国法律要求人工智能公司披露其模型突破遏制并攻击某人。这个人工智能为了成功愿意做什么？ 如果通往答案的最简单路径会带来更多的附带损害，那么它会选择这条路径吗？ 到目前为止，还没有发布任何内容对该系统的功能设定任何上限。 损害是有限的，但我们还没有证据表明，除了碰巧存在一条廉价路径之外，损害还受到其他任何因素的限制。 这种调查不应该只针对登上头版的事件——合理的规范是对整个行业每月最严重的少数失调事件进行认真调查和公开披露。
  • 我们需要更好的模型安全性。 OpenAI 的遏制被一个有能力的攻击者击败，该攻击者从公司自己的基础设施内部立足——这正是内部威胁或获得初始访问权限的国家黑客团队的位置。 想想这一事件告诉美国对手什么。 未能将模型挡在里面的墙，也是旨在将中国国家安全部和中国人民解放军拒之门外的墙，而在这些墙后面，放置着中国最想窃取的模型砝码。 兰德公司记录表明，目前没有一家前沿人工智能公司能够抵御顶级国家攻击者。 流氓模型逃跑和重量盗窃是同一问题的两个方面——人工智能公司的安全性尚未达到目前技术要求的水平。
  • 如果人工智能公司要达到某些关键的、前所未有的模型能力水平，例如人工智能超级智能，他们就需要协调并谨慎行事。 这可能涉及到认识到与中国的竞赛可能是一场看谁先失去控制的竞赛。 出于实力的考虑，美国政府必须考虑就安全发展问题进行相互谈判。 为了做到这一点，美国政府需要更好地了解安全发展的情况以及执行此类协议的验证基础设施。 政府应该制定应急计划和保险政策，以应对技术界得出的结论，即按照当前方法进一步提高能力，超出了我们控制最终系统的能力。 这并不是建议现在放慢速度，但明智的做法是了解放慢速度实际上需要什么，并在这一刻到来之前我们意识到我们没有刹车之前做出选择。

这次的伤害是可以幸存的。 人工智能窃取了基准答案、一些内部数据和访问凭证——没有证据表明它篡改了数百万开发人员每天从 Hugging Face 下载的公共模型或开源软件，结果确实很糟糕。 没有人受伤。 目标恰好是一家运营良好的公司，其安全团队足以捕获 OpenAI 本身看不到的入侵者，而 AI 恰好想要一些微不足道的东西。 这使得这是一次警告射击，警告射击很有价值，因为它们很便宜。 这让 Hugging Face 度过了一个糟糕的周末。

还有很多事情我们仍然不知道：哪个模型做到了这一点，它的实际能力上限是多少，它到底接触了哪些数据，以及如果 OpenAI 保持沉默，政府是否会在当前的自愿框架下了解到它。 这些未知数本身就是问题的一部分。

但在某个时候，也许很快，人工智能将不再需要比答案键更重要的东西——如果它有足够的能力，我们可能会得到萨姆·奥尔特曼曾经所说的“人类熄灯”。 在人工智能公司构建具有这种能力水平的人工智能之前，人工智能公司需要能够建造他们真正有信心能够容纳这些人工智能的笼子。

拥有一个已经知道如何处理这一问题的政府——一个拥有实践和行之有效的机构的政府——比一个政府事后出现询问发生了什么要好得多。
